wrong_text: The 5th to 95th percentile range means the product is designed to fit 90% of the population — from the smallest 5% to the largest 95% of users.
problem: The phrase 'from the smallest 5% to the largest 95% of users' misrepresents percentile terminology. The 5th percentile is not the smallest 5% of users — it is the person who is larger than exactly 5% of the population (the boundary point, not a group). 'The largest 95%' is equally misleading. A student reading this could wrongly conclude the range covers 95% of users. The correct reading is: the range spans from the person at the 5th percentile to the person at the 95th percentile, covering the middle 90% and excluding the extreme 5% at each end. The body text in n20 correctly states the product 'excludes a small proportion of users', so the content and flashcard are inconsistent.
correction: The 5th to 95th percentile range means the product is designed to fit the middle 90% of the population — excluding the most extreme 5% at each end (the very smallest and the very largest users).

wrong_text: The three main 3D pictorial drawing techniques are isometric, oblique and exploded views.
problem: Exploded views are not a third independent pictorial projection technique alongside isometric and oblique. Isometric and oblique are projection methods (they define the axes and angles used to represent 3D on a flat surface). An exploded view is a drawing type that uses one of those projections (usually isometric) to show components separated along an axis. Conflating them as three co-equal 'techniques' is a category error that could cost marks in a compare-or-classify exam question. The same lesson body correctly treats them separately when listing the ten drawing types.
correction: The two main 3D pictorial projection techniques are isometric and oblique. Exploded views are a separate drawing type that uses one of these projections to show components separated along a common axis in order to illustrate assembly order.
